doc.title: Qualified Variables
doc.paragraph: Adaptive Script allows you to declare local and const variables, using the let and const keywords.

Some variables are declared outside of the script, expression, or template that uses them. These variables are read-only and are provided by Adaptive Framework, often to share information about the context the script runs in that may be useful when making a decision. For example, Adaptive Models often evaluate scripts to transform objects and properties, and such a script needs to see the object or property it is transforming. These special, read-only variables are called Qualified Variables.

Qualified Variables take the form qualifier::identifier. The qualifier part of the variable is derived from the context in which the variable is provided. For instance, current::mappedObjectTypeId is a Qualified Variable that is provided by the Adaptive Models when processing an object that is being mapped to another object.

An application's conf may define qualified variables of its own, under qualifiedVariables, as templates. They are compiled when the application conf is loaded or reloaded, and each read of qualifier::name evaluates the compiled template. A #{…} in it already ran when the conf was loaded, a ${…} runs on each read, and a function returned from #{…} runs each time you call it. A template may mix both forms. Templates and Expressions has the details.

When you are debugging, or writing a tool, it can help to see which qualified variables a script can reach right now. qualifier(name) returns a fresh object whose properties are the variables of that qualifier in the current execution context. Each call builds a new object, a snapshot, so it does not change when the variables do. When the qualifier is provided more than once on the stack, the most recent comes first, and older entries only add names not already set. If the qualifier is not active at all, the result is undefined, not an empty object.
qualifiers() returns an object with one property for each active qualifier, holding the same kind of snapshot. A qualifier that is not active is left out, rather than shown as an empty object.

Get (qualifier::name) and snapshots share the same stack and visibility rules: matching frames are walked newest to older, and the first frame that defines a name wins (including a present undefined or null value). Get stops only when a value is found; frames that do not define the name are skipped. Default snapshot visibility matches normal qualifier::name access in the current execution context.

The optional includeUntrusted parameter, false by default, only matters while the context is secure. Set it to true and the snapshot includes the same frames you would see with qualifier::name if you were not secure: the trusted frames and the untrusted ones, not the untrusted ones alone. When the context is already not secure, true and false give the same result, because normal access already sees untrusted frames. Reading qualifier::name is the everyday, fast way; snapshots are not meant for tight loops in production.

Size warning: snapshot objects can get large. Qualifiers such as environment:: and request:: may contribute many properties, and some values can themselves be large. qualifiers() builds a nested object of full snapshots for every active qualifier name and multiplies that cost. Prefer qualifier::name for normal work; use qualifier() / qualifiers() sparingly, and avoid holding or repeatedly rebuilding large snapshots in long-running scripts.

Adaptive Models expose a rich set of current:: variables during on* hooks. The documented set for each hook is the property's contextType (for example modelGetObject or modelGetProperty on model object/property type definitions).
